teaser: Stolen, sawn apart, hidden in a salt mine. One of its panels is still missing.
review_notes:
Jan van Eyck in 1432: court painter to Philip the Good since 1425, diplomatic journey to Portugal 1428-29, house in Bruges bought about 1432, marriage to Margaret about 1432-33: dates approximate.
Philip the Good's 1435 letter to his accountants about Jan's salary ('never find his equal'): paraphrased, check.
Frame inscription naming Hubert (died 1426) as the one who began and Jan as 'second in art', dated 6 May 1432; some scholars question when it was written.
Size open about 3.5 x 4.6 m. Twelve panels, eight wing panels painted on both sides.
Central enthroned figure: God the Father or Christ, debated; lesson says 'God'.
Lamb's original face uncovered by restorers, shown from late 2019/2020.
Eve's fruit as a citrus rather than an apple: common reading.
Adam and Eve removed after 1781 (Joseph II); clothed copies made in the 1860s.
History: central panels in Paris 1794-1815; wings sold 1816, later Berlin; returned after the Treaty of Versailles; found in the Altaussee salt mine, 1945.
1934 theft of the Just Judges; ransom of one million Belgian francs; Arsène Goedertier's deathbed claim; copy by Jef Van der Veken finished 1945.
Whether this photograph shows the lamb before or after restoration cannot be judged at this size; no spot depends on it.

lesson.text: For Jan van Eyck, 1432 was a very good year. He was in his forties, court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, one of the richest rulers in Europe. He drew a yearly salary whether he painted or not. He had recently come back from a diplomatic trip to Portugal, was buying a house in Bruges, and married a woman named Margaret around this time.

That May he also delivered the largest job of his life, to a church in Ghent. Oddly, it was not entirely his. A verse on the frame says the painter Hubert van Eyck began the work and that Jan, his brother, “second in art,” finished it. Hubert had died in 1426. Not one other painting by him is known for certain.

The duke trusted Jan with secret missions abroad and treated him as more than a craftsman. When his accountants tried to trim the painter's salary, Philip wrote to stop them, warning that he would never find another artist his equal.

The altarpiece is a folding cupboard of pictures, about 3.5 meters high and 4.6 wide when open (roughly 11 by 15 ft). On ordinary days the wings stayed shut. On feast days they swung apart and showed what you see here: twelve panels in two rows. Begin upstairs, with the giants.

lesson.title: The upper row
lesson.text: Seven figures larger than life. Four details show what was new.

spots.title: A crown on the floor
spots.text: At the feet of God, enthroned in red, lies a gold crown heavy with pearls and gems. Each stone has its own tiny highlight, as if lit from a real window.

spots.title: The choir
spots.text: A tight group of angels sings from one book. Their brows wrinkle and their mouths open differently. An early writer claimed you could tell from each face which voice it sang.

spots.title: The organ
spots.text: Metal pipes in strict rows, each with its own reflection. The angel at the keyboard wears stiff brocade, a heavy silk woven with gold thread.

spots.title: Adam's foot
spots.text: Adam's toes stick out past the edge of his stone niche, seen slightly from below. The panel hung high, so that is how a real foot would look from the church floor.

lesson.text: Sparkle, reflection, skin: none of this was possible with the egg-based paint most artists used. The Van Eycks mixed their colors with oil, which dries slowly and can be laid in thin see-through layers called glazes. Light passes through them and bounces back, so a ruby glows from inside. They did not invent oil paint. They showed what it could do.

The Ghent Altarpiece is where European painting learned to imitate the look of the world: the shine of metal, the weight of cloth, the pores of skin. For the next 400 years, oil would be the painter's main tool.

Downstairs the scale changes completely. Hundreds of small figures gather in a meadow, and the same horizon runs across all five lower panels as if the frames were windows onto one country. Where is everyone going? The composition answers with geometry.
Every group in the lower row is aimed at the same point.

lines.label: The central axis
lines.text: One vertical runs through God's face, the dove in its burst of light, the lamb on the altar and the fountain. Heaven and the meadow are pinned together.

lines.label: From the front
lines.text: Two packed crowds kneel and stand in the foreground, prophets on the left, apostles and churchmen in red on the right. They open like a V toward the altar.

lines.label: From the back
lines.text: Two more processions come out of the trees behind: bishops on the left, women saints carrying palm branches on the right.

lines.label: From the wings
lines.text: Even the side panels join in. Riders arrive from the left, hermits and pilgrims on foot from the right. All humanity converges.

lesson.text: At the point where the lines meet stands a lamb on an altar, bleeding calmly into a gold cup. It is a symbol for Christ, sacrificed like the lambs of ancient ritual. This is why the whole work is also called the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb. In front, a fountain spills the water of life toward you.

During a long restoration, conservators found that the lamb's head had been painted over in the 1500s. Underneath was Van Eyck's original: a face with forward-looking, almost human eyes. When photos came out, the internet could not decide whether it was moving or alarming.

Go back up to the far ends of the top row. Adam and Eve are among the first life-size nudes in northern European painting, and they are not idealized statues. They look like two real people who have undressed. Each covers up with a hand or a leaf. One of them holds the evidence.
The first sin involved a piece of fruit. Who has it, and where?

spots.title: Eve's fruit
spots.text: Eve raises it in her right hand. It is small, yellowish and knobbly, more like a citrus than the round red apple of later pictures. The Bible never says which fruit it was.

lesson.text: That frankness caused trouble. In 1781 an emperor visiting Ghent found the two nudes improper, and they were taken down. In the 1800s the church hung copies in their place in which Adam and Eve wear animal skins. The originals spent decades in a Brussels museum before they came home.

And that is a mild episode. The altarpiece was hidden from rioters who smashed church images in 1566. French troops carried the middle panels to Paris in 1794. The wings were sold in 1816 and ended up in Berlin. Germany had to give them back after the First World War. It is often called the most stolen artwork in history.

In the Second World War the altarpiece was seized for Hitler's planned museum. American soldiers found it in 1945, deep inside a salt mine in the Austrian Alps, stacked among thousands of other looted works.

One theft was never undone. On an April night in 1934, someone removed the lower left panel, the Just Judges, and demanded a million Belgian francs. The ransom was not paid. Months later a local stockbroker said on his deathbed that he alone knew where it was, and died without telling. What you see in its place is a copy, finished in 1945.

spots.title: The Just Judges
spots.text: Riders in rich furs on a rocky road. This is the replacement, painted by the restorer Jef Van der Veken. The original has been missing since 1934.

spots.title: The Knights of Christ
spots.text: Young knights in polished armor carry lances with banners. Their white horse steps forward with an arched neck.

spots.title: A giant pilgrim
spots.text: Leading the pilgrims is a man a head taller than everyone else, wrapped in red. He is Saint Christopher, whom legend describes as a giant and who protects travelers.

spots.title: The hermits
spots.text: Bearded men in dark, rough robes with walking sticks and prayer beads. Two women peer out from the rocks behind them.

spots.title: Red robes
spots.text: Popes and bishops stand in a block of scarlet, crowned with jeweled headgear. The painters gave each a different face.

spots.title: The dove
spots.text: A dove in a ring of light, sign of the Holy Spirit. Fine gold rays fan out from it over the entire meadow.

spots.title: The fountain
spots.text: An eight-sided stone basin with a bronze column. Its overflow runs in a little channel straight toward the bottom of the frame, and toward you.

spots.title: The first murder
spots.text: Above Eve, painted to look like carved stone: her son Cain killing his brother Abel. Sin, the panel says, did not stop at the fruit.

lesson.text: Today the altarpiece stands in St Bavo's Cathedral in Ghent, the same church it was painted for, inside a climate-controlled glass case. A restoration that began in 2012 has been removing old overpaint panel by panel, and colors unseen for centuries are coming back.

Remember the verse on the frame: Jan, in his best year and at the top of his trade, called himself second and gave first place to a dead brother. Six centuries later nobody can say for sure which brushstrokes belong to whom.

quiz.question: According to the verse on the frame, who began the altarpiece?
quiz.explanation: The inscription says Hubert began it and Jan, 'second in art,' completed it in 1432.

quiz.question: What made the Van Eycks' glowing colors possible?
options: Thin see-through layers of oil paint
quiz.explanation: Oil glazes let light pass through and bounce back.

quiz.question: What stands at the point where all the crowds converge?
quiz.explanation: The lamb, a symbol of Christ, is the target of every procession.

quiz.question: Which panel is a copy, because the original was stolen in 1934?
quiz.explanation: The Just Judges disappeared in 1934 and has never been found.

quiz.question: Where did American soldiers find the altarpiece in 1945?
options: In a salt mine in the Austrian Alps
In the tower of the cathedral
quiz.explanation: It had been stored underground with thousands of other looted works.

quiz.question: What did restorers discover about the lamb?
options: It had originally been a lion
Its original, almost human face had been painted over
quiz.explanation: A 16th-century overpaint hid Van Eyck's original head.

facts.text: The Van Eyck brothers invented oil paint.
facts.explanation: Oil paint already existed. They showed how much it could do.

facts.text: Copies of Adam and Eve wearing animal skins once replaced the nude originals.
facts.explanation: The nudes were judged improper and clothed copies were hung in the 1800s.

facts.text: The stolen Just Judges panel was recovered after the ransom was paid.
facts.explanation: The ransom was not paid and the panel is still missing.
